titre: The Myth of the Eight Swallowed Spiders
accroche: The claim that we swallow eight spiders a year in our sleep has circulated for decades. No study has ever measured it.
contenu_vulgarise:
One number keeps coming back, in several versions: the average sleeper supposedly swallows eight spiders a year (sometimes four a year, sometimes twenty in a lifetime, depending on which version is going around). The number changes, the claim stays, and it has ended up as a “fact” people pull out at parties without a second thought.

Yet no study measures it. Rod Crawford, curator of arachnology at the Burke Museum at the University of Washington, has for decades kept a page devoted to the most widespread myths about spiders. On this one in particular, his finding is clear: no such case is recorded in the scientific or medical literature. No verified study, no photo, no collected specimen, no medical record, no proven observation. After millions of nights shared with millions of sleepers, not a single witness.

## What a Spider Knows About a Sleeper

Biology explains this silence. A spider perceives the world first through vibrations: that is how it detects prey caught in its web, an approaching predator, or any danger at all. A sleeping human is not a neutral signal in this respect. Breathing, pulse, and any snoring produce a steady pounding of vibrations, exactly the kind of signal a spider associates with a threat to flee, not with prey to approach.

Bill Shear, an arachnologist at Hampden-Sydney College and a former president of the American Arachnological Society, sums up the disproportion of scale: to a spider, a human falls into the same category as a rock, a feature of the landscape, neither edible nor of any interest. Nothing in the documented behavior of spiders drives them to actively seek out an open human mouth.

## What Remains Once the Number Is Set Aside

This myth does not teach us much about spiders: mostly it shows how a “fact” can stand on repetition alone. The figure of eight has circulated for so long, in so many slightly different variants, that its apparent precision, an easy number to remember, hides the complete absence of any source behind it. No one has measured it, because measuring an event that requires you to be unaware of it while it happens is, by construction, impossible: noticing it would mean no longer being asleep.

The myth survives, then, less through biological plausibility (there is none) than through the very shape of the story: unprovable by construction, it also cannot be contradicted by a personal experience that would disprove it. A claim tailor-made never to meet its own denial, which paradoxically makes it harder to dislodge than a myth you could at least check for yourself.

citation.texte: A sleeping person is not something a spider would willingly approach.

carte.punch: You have never swallowed a single spider in your sleep.
carte.idee: The claim that we swallow eight spiders a year in our sleep has circulated for decades without any study, medical case, or observation to support it. Spiders perceive our vibrations as a danger to flee, not as prey to approach.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: In English; dozens of spider myths, each handled in one short page.

quiz.question: Why does a spider have, biologically, no reason to approach a sleeping person?
choix: Because the smell of the human body acts on it as a natural repellent
Because its fangs are physically too small to pierce human skin
Because it perceives the vibrations of breathing and pulse as a signal of danger, not of prey
Because the body heat given off during sleep makes it flee
quiz.explication: Spiders perceive the world mostly through vibrations, which they use to detect prey and predators. Those of a sleeper (breathing, pulse, snoring) signal a danger to flee, not prey to approach; at a spider's scale, a human is a feature of the landscape, like a rock.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who is Rod Crawford, and what does he say about this myth?
choix: An emergency physician who has tallied several documented clinical cases
A curator of arachnology who finds no documented case of the myth
A science journalist who invented the figure of eight spiders
A biologist who ran the first statistical study on the subject
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A curator of arachnology at the Burke Museum, Rod Crawford finds a complete absence of documented cases in the literature.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Bill Shear, how does a spider perceive a human being, at its scale?
choix: As a formidable predator to be fled at all costs
As a particularly attractive source of heat
As potential prey, but too large to attack
As a feature of the landscape, neither edible nor of any interest, like a rock
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Bill Shear compares the disproportion of scale: to a spider, a human falls into the same category as a rock.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why, according to the card, is this myth especially hard to check through personal experience?
choix: Because no laboratory has ever agreed to fund a study on the subject
Because an event you are unaware of while asleep cannot be observed
Because spiders leave no detectable genetic trace after digestion
Because the number of spiders varies too much across regions of the world
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Measuring an event that requires you to be unaware of it while it happens is, by construction, impossible.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Besides eight spiders a year, which variants of the figure circulate, according to the card?
choix: Two a month, or a hundred in a lifetime
One a week, or fifty a year
Four a year, or twenty in a lifetime
Sixteen a year, or just one in a lifetime
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card cites two other versions of the same myth: four spiders a year, or twenty in a lifetime.
